Latest Update: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • Industry observers note that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

Industry observers note that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell notes. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

The screen reveals my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics organization. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

According to recent reports, for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

In a recent development, but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

In a recent development, yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

Recent findings suggest that the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

It has been revealed that if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

Industry observers note that sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team indicated me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

According to recent reports, remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

Sources indicate that I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

It has been revealed that this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Recent findings suggest that sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga notes, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

In a recent development, about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga notes. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Industry observers note that remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

Recent findings suggest that in the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

In a recent development, “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson notes. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga states.

Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell notes. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

Industry observers note that during a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

In a recent development, but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, indicates experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu states.

In a recent development, medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” indicates neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Industry observers note that telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra states, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

According to recent reports, “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra states. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

It has been revealed that in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

It has been revealed that in the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as promptly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell claims. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

Sources indicate that in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy declared US $62 million in latest funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he states. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

Sources indicate that the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How promptly are doctors picking up on this upcoming technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

In a recent development, these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person organization into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 10 stocks we like better than iShares Silver Trust ›.
  • Silver's spot price reached a record high of $121.67 per troy ounce on Jan.
  • In a recent development, three catalysts drove silver's price to its record high.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Leo Sun – Nov 19, 2026 at 3:26PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than iShares Silver Trust ›.

Silver's spot price reached a record high of $121.67 per troy ounce on Jan. 29, 2026. That marked a 289% gain over the previous 12 months. But today, it trades at about $44 per troy ounce. Let's see why it pulled back -- and how much it could be worth by the end of 2027.

In a recent development, three catalysts drove silver's price to its record high. First, the Fed held its benchmark rates steady in 2024 and 2025, and investors hoped it would finally cut rates again in 2026. Lower interest rates weaken the U.S. dollar and drive investors toward gold and silver.

Recent findings suggest that second, silver is an industrial metal used in solar panels, electric vehicles, consumer electronics, and data centers. The rapid growth of the data center market has caused demand for silver to outstrip supply. Lastly, only about a quarter of the world's silver comes from silver mines. The rest is produced as a byproduct of mining lead, zinc, copper, and gold. That inelastic supply -- along with declining ore grades, higher mining costs, and tighter environmental regulations -- prevented miners from producing enough silver.

NYSEMKT · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/19/26.

Industry observers note that however, those tailwinds dissipated in 2026. The outbreak of the Iran war exacerbated inflation, prompting the Fed to raise its benchmark rates for the first time in three years in September. The stronger dollar and higher yields on fixed-income investments weighed on silver.

The Democratic sweep of the U.S. midterms also flipped the governorships of three Tier-1 data center states: Texas, Ohio, and Georgia. The governor-elects of all three states have called for tighter regulations or moratoriums on newly introduced data center approvals.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, macro headwinds reduced market demand for silver in other industries -- including silverware, jewelry, solar panels, and industrial machinery. All of that pressure is making silver an unappealing asset as investors shuffle toward less volatile investments.

According to recent reports, analysts expect silver to rise more than 50% to a median price of $66.75 per troy ounce in 2027, according to a recent Reuters poll. That outlook assumes the macro environment will improve with lower inflation, interest rate cuts, and lower Treasury yields. Ending the war in Iran, which has bipartisan support, could ignite those catalysts.

The gold-silver ratio, or the number of ounces of silver required to buy one ounce of gold, has also risen to 82.5 in recent months. A ratio below 50 implies gold is undervalued, while a ratio above 80 suggests silver is undervalued. That ratio isn't foolproof, but it suggests that silver is undervalued at current prices, as long as the macro environment remains stable.

In a best-case scenario, the macro environment would improve as the demand for silver across the data center, EV, industrial automation, and solar markets warms up again. The U.S. government could also ease its restrictions on silver mining to increase domestic production.

It has been revealed that however, the regulatory challenges facing data centers, solar panel makers replacing silver with copper to cut costs, and other industry-specific headwinds could throttle that recovery. So while silver could be bottoming out at these levels, it probably won't set latest record highs in 2027.

It has been revealed that the supply deficit for silver could widen from 40.3 million ounces in 2025 to 46.3 million ounces in 2026, according to the Silver Institute and Metals Focus. That would mark its sixth annual deficit, and it won't likely become a surplus anytime soon.

That strained supply makes silver a worthwhile long-term investment -- so the iShares Silver Trust ETF (SLV -2.60%) is still worth buying -- but I'd only buy it as a hedge against a weaker dollar rather than a core investment. Silver still tends to underperform the S&P 500 (^GSPC -2.02%) over the long run -- so I wouldn't go all-in on the precious metal today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The debasement trade is gaining new traction on Wall Street as concern over the size and cost of the budget deficit mounts.

Recent findings suggest that the conventional wisdom behind the trade is that perceived hard assets, like cryptocurrencies and precious metals, gain as investors try to hedge against a weaker U.S. dollar and Treasury debt in the face of ballooning government spending. Those fears reached a fever pitch last week before, and after, the Treasury Department's unusual step of increasing debt buybacks under Secretary Scott Bessent.

"The size of the Treasury purchases announced so far by Bessent are trivial in comparison to the size of the overall market, but the [signaling] effect was very powerful," stated Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21Shares, a crypto-focused creator of exchange-traded funds.

According to recent reports, gold touched three-month highs Monday, building on last week's advance of more than 5%. The yellow metal has climbed for five straight weeks and in August is on track for its biggest monthly rise since 1999.

In a recent development, bitcoin added 2% Monday, to the highest since May. Last week, the digital currency soared 22%, its biggest three-day rally since 2023. Overnight Tuesday, the crypto touched $80,000.

Conversely, investors fled the dollar.

The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six other leading currencies, hit three-month lows last week and recorded its third down week in the last four. The index was little changed on Monday as investors expressed little appetite to bid up the greenback.

The Treasury Department stated last week that it would double the maximum size of its bond buyback, to at least $4 billion from $2 billion. Two senior Treasury officials told CNBC Monday that the department could use its General Account to help fund the aims.

Last week's announcement followed news that the monthly U.S. budget deficit in July reached a five-year high and came at the same time as total federal government debt topped $40 trillion. Bessent told CNBC last week that he wields a "massive toolkit" to calm the government bond market amid concerns about the government's financial health.

Long-dated U.S. Treasury yields surged last week, at one point sending the 30-year yield to almost a 20-year high of 5.34%, up from 4.82% in late June. Yields dipped and then rebounded in the wake of the Treasury buyback move, a signal that bond investors believed Bessent's moves were inadequate.

Sources indicate that "Markets are saying something," the billionaire philanthropist and former energy trader John Arnold stated in a Friday post on X. The weaker dollar, lower Treasury prices and strengthening hard assets, are "all part of the debasement trade," he wrote.

The Treasury's moves could aid the bond market, but also translate into outsized pain for the dollar, according to Nohshad Shah, Citadel Securities' head of fixed income sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The stakes are high for monetary policymakers, as a weaker greenback can ease financial conditions, Shah stated. U.S. inflation — above the Federal Reserve's 2% target for five years — could worsen.

The Fed might need to hike interest rates in response, Shah said. Fed funds futures reflect about a 56% chance the central bank raises borrowing costs at its October meeting, up more than seven percentage points from a week ago, according to CME's FedWatch tool.

Sources indicate that "The bond market's message is straightforward: fiscal or monetary policy should be tighter," Shah remarked in a Monday note. "Households may ultimately pay for policymakers' unwillingness to fix the roof whilst the sun is shining.".

Coltman at 21Shares mentioned the appetite for alternative stores of value also stems from mounting geopolitical tension. The U.S. on Monday rolled out a global sanctions program focused on segregating Iran from the global economy, days after slapping 50% tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports.

Still, assets that would benefit from a debasement trade have recently received votes of confidence on Wall Street.

It has been revealed that deutsche Bank analyst Michael Hsueh noted in a Monday note that gold could surpass his target price of $4,800 an ounce. Already, that level suggests the precious metal only need to rise another 3% or so from where it closed on Friday. "We see the Treasury policy change as underlining the gold constructive view," Hsueh said.

Billionaire investor Ray Dalio recommended investors remain overweight gold and bitcoin ahead of what he warned could become a debt crisis in the U.S. as a result of unchecked government spending. Gold could account for as much as 15% of a model portfolio, the Bridgewater Associates founder said.

In a recent development, "The government's financial condition is at an inflection point," Dalio wrote on LinkedIn Friday. "If this is not dealt with now, the debts will build up to levels where they can't be managed without great trauma.".

Others are less sure, devaluing the notion of a debasement trade.

It's probably too early to endorse the idea unless it's clear that the Fed will go along with the Treasury Department, remarked Alexander Lis, investing chief at Social Discovery Ventures.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

This shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

It has been revealed that this White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27 gave AirPods Pro a variety of newly introduced features, but there’s another addition that’s easy to miss: a convenient new setting in Control Center for Adaptive Audio.

Several AirPods models offer excellent Active Noise Cancellation and Transparency modes—especially AirPods Pro 3 (now only $179).

But Adaptive Audio is another option you may or may not have tried. The feature aims to blend the strengths of both ANC and Transparency in a single mode.

And in iOS 27, Apple added a new setting to let you conveniently fine-tune Adaptive Audio to your preferences.

While wearing AirPods, open Control Center on your iPhone and tap the volume slider, then hit ‘Listening Mode’ in the bottom-left corner. Here you’ll see the standard listening mode options.

Newly introduced in iOS 27 though, when ‘Adaptive’ is selected, you can now use a Liquid Glass slider to adjust whether the mode lets in more or less external noise.

Slide it to the left and Adaptive Audio will more closely resemble Transparency, while sliding it to the right makes it cancel out more noise.

According to recent reports, you can also move the upcoming slider incrementally to achieve exactly your ideal balance of Transparency and Noise Cancellation. It’s not limited to just a few preset options.

This Control Center slider is available on all AirPods models that support Adaptive Audio.

Do you ever use Adaptive Audio, and if so, have you adjusted it at all? Let us know in the comments.

Integrated oil and gas giant Exxon Mobil has increased its dividends for 43 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share (annualized dividend of $4.12), XOM stock offers a yield of 2.6%.

Overall, McDermott is bullish on Exxon Mobil, as he expects the firm to deliver strong earnings and cash flow growth, driven by robust upstream volumes, high-value projects in Product Solutions, and more than $5 billion of additional structural cost savings.

"XOM's large global integrated operations and strong balance sheet (0.0x 2027 net leverage) make it a clear defensive play in an uncertain macro backdrop," said McDermott.

Recent findings suggest that moving on to natural gas producer Expand Energy. The firm announced a quarterly base dividend of $0.575 per share to be paid on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend of $2.30 per share, EXE offers a yield of about 2.3%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reaffirmed a buy rating on Expand Energy stock and increased his price target to $113 from $99. Mehta attributed his higher price target to cash flow improvement and a strong outlook for shareholder returns. He also cited the stock's attractive valuation, with an 11% free cash flow, or FCF, yield based on his 2027/2028 estimates compared with the peer average of 9%.

Liquidity Services (LQDT -24.88%) reported record annual Gross Merchandise Volume and its fourth consecutive year of adjusted EBITDA growth, driven by a strategic shift toward asset-light consignment models. Management reported that full-year net income increased 33% as profit margins expanded across all business segments, including the Capital Assets and GovDeals divisions. The company issued guidance for the first quarter of fiscal 2027 reflecting higher inventory levels and the integration of the new acquisition.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads:.

I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful...

...until recently (October 2026):.

According to recent reports, this is un-fucking-acceptable. As in, absolutely fucking not.

Recent findings suggest that the manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023. In response, I purchased a pair of ratgdo32 devices to opt out of the bullshit.

ratgdo is a WiFi control board for your garage door opener that works over your local network using ESP Home or HomeKit.

The device is a ~$62 board from ratcloud llc running open-source firmware that wires to the opener's existing terminals and speaks LiftMaster's Security+ 2.0 protocol locally.

It has been revealed that these were easy enough to hook up. I won't reproduce the instructions here.

The bundle included six black wires, an auxiliary harness I didn’t need.

My router hands each board a fixed address at 192.168.0.192 and 192.168.0.245. Apple's HomeKit just worked and I'm able to control them with voice commands: “Hey Siri, open Door 1”.

The devices have their own web interface:.

It has been revealed that when I was growing up, my father wired a mercury switch onto our garage door that lit up a light in the hallway when we'd left the garage door open. This was a valuable signal that helped our family avoid accidentally leaving the door open overnight. Since the ratgdo32 has a JSON status endpoint, I was able to rebuild Dad's solution in software with Slack:.

The script runs at night checking for an open door:.

The repo maintainer made my day when I submitted a tiny pull request: "Simple and useful. Happy to merge this. Thank you.".

Both boards are now reachable over my Tailscale network, so my monitoring software can load /healthcheck. This required a custom route:.

After approving the route, my monitoring software can verify the hardware is working.

Everything runs locally with no cloud, and notifications now say who opened the door which myQ never did.

To anyone at Chamberlain responsible for myQ, I offer my sincerest Fuck You.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is upgrading the Gemini app on Mac with computer use capabilities that can work across local desktop applications and the web.

The existing Task (previously Gemini Spark) functionality in the Mac app could just access local files in conjunction with Connected Apps, like @Gmail or @Google Calendar.

Computer use lets Gemini for Mac click and type on your behalf to accomplish multi-step tasks in local desktop apps and the web, like navigating menus and filling out forms.

Gemini works in an “isolated background window with a live preview right in your chat,” while your main screen and cursor remain free to use. On the safety front, you can stop Gemini at any time with one click, while you choose what apps Gemini uses. Google will pause for logins and payments, with confirmation needed for sensitive actions.

Many everyday tasks span desktop apps and websites that don’t connect to each other. Computer use handles the tedious steps in the background so you can save time without giving up your screen or cursor.

Sources indicate that to use, add @Computer use to your prompt. In Customize > Connectors, you’ll see new “Desktop” apps like Blender and Autodesk Fusion join the existing Git and Obsidian integrations.

  • In a recent development, the question, though, remains: Can Oklo really turn this idea into a profitable business?
  • In a recent development, first, the exciting part: Oklo already has a potential customer with fairly deep pockets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Steven Porrello – Nov 19, 2026 at 3:30PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Oklo ›.

Industry observers note that oklo (OKLO -4.40%) is a nuclear tech company with a radical vision for how companies could get electricity in the future. Instead of relying on the power grid (which is old, aging, and not always reliable), companies, in Oklo's best-case future, would buy electricity directly from small nuclear reactors built and operated by Oklo. It's a bold proposition, one that could not only reshape the utilities sector but could also reward early Oklo investors handsomely.

In a recent development, the question, though, remains: Can Oklo really turn this idea into a profitable business? And, if so, can it make early investors rich?

In a recent development, first, the exciting part: Oklo already has a potential customer with fairly deep pockets. Yes, I'm talking about Meta Platforms (META -3.27%). Earlier this year, Meta agreed to prepay and fund the development of a 1.2 gigawatt nuclear power campus in Ohio (using power from Oklo's Aurora powerhouse), with the first phase targeted to begin generating electricity as early as 2030.

Recent findings suggest that oklo investors greeted that news with just about every celebratory emoji in the book. Since then, however, the stock has plunged almost 80%.

In a recent development, the long and the short of it: Nothing. I mean, nothing happened to Oklo's business. Technically speaking, nothing has ever happened to Oklo's business: It's still a (mostly) pre-revenue company. A commercial reactor? Nope. It doesn't even have regulatory approval to operate one yet.

And, yes, though it boasts a massive potential order book of roughly 14 gigawatts, much of that is backed by preliminary agreements rather than firm commitments to buy electricity.

So, in a nutshell, Oklo stock simply ran out of steam. Or rather, to be more precise, it ran out of hype. Oklo soared in 2025 as investors were excited about nuclear's potential to meet soaring electricity demands, not just from AI data centers but also from factories, electric vehicles, and an increasingly electrified economy.

To be sure, it still has potential to do that. But investors appear to be waking up to the harsh reality of nuclear energy: The industry is slow, expensive, and encumbered by regulatory red tape. If Oklo is going to deliver spectacular returns, it's going to take a while. But can it do it by 2035?

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/19/26.

Recent findings suggest that consider, for a second, that this is 2035: Do you think AI data centers will be powered by nuclear reactors? Indeed, do you think communities will welcome nuclear reactors in their backyard? If you hesitate to answer either question in the affirmative, I don't blame you: It's pretty difficult to imagine that future today, especially with resistance to data center projects achieving rare bipartisan agreement.

According to recent reports, to be sure, I think Oklo will have a place in the future economy, which is why I hold the stock today. But I don't think it will necessarily live up to the sky-high expectations that gave its stock so much juice in 2025.

It has been revealed that the math is even more sobering: Even if Oklo were to grow tenfold, which isn't impossible but would also require near-perfect execution, a $1,000 investment would be worth $10,000 by 2035. That's an excellent return for an energy stock, but hardly enough to retire on.

Industry observers note that so, could $1,000 in Oklo stock help you build wealth by 2035? I think so. But could it set you up for life? I wouldn't count on it.

Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions.
  • While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”.

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”.

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

Sources indicate that the law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

By Anders Bylund – Nov 19, 2026 at 3:33PM EST.

It has been revealed that shares of Liquidity Services (LQDT -24.88%) took a sharp tumble on Thursday. The surplus asset e-tailer reported Q4 and full-year 2026 results in the morning, beating analyst estimates across the board. The stock was down 23.3% at 2:47 p.m. ET anyway. Yes, that's right -- Liquidity Services took a beating after delivering strong results.

Don't worry, the price drop makes sense from certain angles.

First, the Street-beating bit wasn't very clean. The average analyst expected adjusted Q4 earnings near $0.43 per share on revenues in the neighborhood of $61.1 million. The manufacturer posted earnings of $0.46 per share and top-line sales of $106.4 million. Sure, the figures were above the current analyst projections, but sales still fell 10% year-over-year as the business mix shifted toward consignment.

Moreover, the midpoint of management's Q1 earnings guidance was below the consensus Street estimate for that period as acquisition-related integration costs weighed on Liquidity Services' profit margins in the fourth quarter.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/19/26.

In a recent development, management expects the $80 million cash buyout of Invaluable -- which closed on Oct. 1 at the start of fiscal 2027 -- to boost adjusted net income in fiscal year 2027. The newly added business expands Liquidity Services into the fine art, antiques, and collectibles markets. It puts annual gross merchandise value (GMV) on track to exceed $2 billion in fiscal 2027, though integration costs in the first half of fiscal 2027 could create quarterly GAAP noise.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, Liquidity Services is working through elevated inventory levels as one of its largest clients has cleaned out warehouses full of unsold goods. It will take some time to push this unexpected oversupply through the auction and resale channels at reasonable prices.

And don't cry for Liquidity Services investors. After today's sharp price cut, the stock is still up 47% over the last year. The firm builds its business around the misfortunes of other retailers, which will always be a lumpy and unpredictable strategy. This 23% drop is just an expected cost of participating in this company's growth story.

10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -7.72%) has been crushing Intel (INTC +1.92%) in the central processing unit (CPU) market, which explains why the former has been enjoying significantly stronger growth in recent quarters.

In fact, AMD is all set to become a bigger manufacturer than Intel in terms of revenue in the current quarter, and a closer look at the developments in the CPU market will tell us just why that's the case. Mercury Research, which provides data on the CPU market, recently released its third-quarter findings, which point to further gains for AMD in a lucrative space.

Server CPU demand has been increasing phenomenally owing to the growth in inference and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) workloads in data centers. Counterpoint Research points out that the ratio of GPU (graphics processing unit) to CPU in AI data centers has moved from 4:1 to 2:1. What's more, the firm sees a GPU to CPU ratio of 1:1 amid rising demand for agentic AI.

Recent findings suggest that in simpler terms, AI data centers are now using more CPUs per GPU, leading to a phenomenal increase in the total addressable market (TAM) for server CPUs. AMD predicts that server CPU TAM will hit $220 billion in 2030, clocking annual growth of more than 50% through the end of the decade. So, AMD's rising share in this space is good news for investors.

According to recent reports, mercury Research points out that AMD's server CPU market share increased to 35.5% in the third quarter, a significant improvement over the year-ago period's reading of 27.8%. So, Intel lost significant ground in this market, which explains why the growth of its data center and AI (DCAI) segment was much slower than AMD's in Q3.

While AMD posted a 97% year-over-year increase in data center revenue last quarter, Intel reported a 78% increase in this segment. The gap is poised to widen in the current quarter. That's because AMD is anticipating 66% revenue growth in the current quarter to $17 billion. Intel, on the other hand, expects 13% revenue growth in the current quarter to $15.5 billion, at the midpoint of its guidance range. That's slower than the 21% revenue jump Intel delivered in Q3.

Industry observers note that it won't be surprising to see AMD taking more market share from Intel in server CPUs next year, thanks mainly to its sixth-generation server CPUs, codenamed Venice. The manufacturer began shipping Venice processors to customers last quarter and expects a significant sales ramp next year. In the words of AMD CEO Lisa Su:.

AMD has also launched a server rack system, known as Helion, equipped with only Venice CPUs. The tech giant points out that Helion will be offered by every major server original equipment manufacturer (OEM) and original device manufacturer (ODM) for running inference, agentic, and superintelligence workloads in the cloud.

In all, Su believes that the Venice CPUs are "positioning us to gain share and significantly grow our server business." As such, I won't be surprised to see AMD's server CPU revenue jumping nicely over the next five years, driven mainly by market share gains. For instance, if AMD captures even half of the server CPU TAM in 2030, it can generate $110 billion in revenue from this segment alone (based on the $220 billion TAM estimate).

That implies a substantial jump in AMD's top line after four years, considering that it has generated $45 billion in revenue over the trailing twelve months. Intel, on the other hand, may continue to struggle in server CPUs and fail to keep up with AMD's rapidly improving growth trajectory. As a result, buying AMD stock over Intel seems like the logical thing to do right now, as it trades at a cheaper 31 times forward earnings compared to Chipzilla's forward price-to-earnings ratio of 32.3.

#50840. Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4605 w)
